executive_summary: The defining story of the day is the fracturing of the Republican establishment, most sharply illustrated by Ken Paxton's defeat of incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Texas Senate runoff — a result that signals MAGA-aligned insurgents can now topple sitting members of the U.S. Senate, not merely challenge them. The New York Times newsletter flagged the Texas showdown as the evening's central political event, and the breaking news confirmed the outcome as a genuine upset, reinforcing that the GOP's internal civil war has entered a more consequential phase. The Economist's note that America's economy is soaring 'even with the MAGA tax' adds critical context: the establishment wing of the party can no longer rely on economic credibility as a shield against populist challenges, because voters in today's Republican primary are prioritizing ideological loyalty over governing competence. Taken together, these signals point to a party whose center of gravity has shifted decisively, with downstream consequences for Senate leadership, legislative dealmaking, and the 2026 midterm landscape.

newsletters.title: A French Open fit for Fashion Week

items.headline: Osaka's latest tennis couture
items.blurb: At the French Open on Tuesday, the four-time Grand Slam champion staged an outfit reveal once again ahead of her first-round match against Germany's Laura Siegemund. Osaka wore a black corset and a matching pleated, cascading skirt that skimmed over the clay, layered over a gold dress designed by Nike, striped with sequins which shimmered and sparkled in the Paris sunshine. The Nike dress glittered so much in the bright afternoon sun it looked more like a figure skating outfit than the average tennis getup.

items.headline: Gauff's newest opponent? Her mind
items.blurb: Watching Coco Gauff's shots during her first-round match at the French Open against Taylor Townsend, and most of her matches of late, doesn't tell the whole story. Watch her eyes. Watch her shoulders. Watch her racket. She hit herself on the head with it in the middle of the Italian Open final against Elina Svitolina two Sundays ago. It's been that kind of nine months for Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam champion, and at 22, the biggest star in the women's game.

newsletters.title: The Evening: Republican showdown in Texas

items.headline: Texans head to the polls, again
items.blurb: Texas Republicans right now are casting votes in a runoff between the incumbent Senator John Cornyn and Ken Paxton, the MAGA-aligned state attorney general. Follow our live coverage and the results, as they come in. Tonight's election, the most expensive primary runoff in recent history, could decide whether Republicans keep control of the Senate. Some Republicans worry that a victory by the hard-line Paxton, who has led in recent polls, could become a liability in the general election. The winner will face the Democratic nominee, James Talarico. Cornyn is fighting for his political life against Paxton, who has been impeached and indicted on securities fraud charges but was nonetheless endorsed last week by President Trump. Trump has used his endorsements to oust Republicans he saw as insufficiently loyal, including Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana.

items.headline: A federal court rejected Alabama's new voting map for the midterm elections
items.blurb: A federal court rejected Alabama's new voting map for the midterm elections, saying it discriminated against Black people. Alabama is likely to appeal the ruling.

items.headline: South Carolina's state senate refused to approve a new Trump-backed voting map
items.blurb: South Carolina's state senate refused to approve a new Trump-backed voting map that aimed to eliminate the state's only majority-Black district.

items.headline: A judge temporarily let stand an aggressive new Florida voting map
items.blurb: A judge temporarily let stand an aggressive new Florida voting map as a lawsuit against it moves forward. The map could give Republicans four additional seats.

items.headline: U.S. and Iran resume hostilities despite peace talks
items.blurb: Trump over the weekend announced that a deal to end the war with Iran was nigh. But in the days since, fighting has continued. Iran deployed mine-laying boats in the Strait of Hormuz and flew attack drones near U.S. ships, American officials said. Then the U.S. military attacked Iranian boats and missile-launch sites in what it called "self-defense strikes." The Trump administration has given mixed signals on the state of play. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said today that talks to end the war were ongoing, and that a deal could take "a few days." The president has focused on a preliminary deal to reopen the strait — yet other issues, like what to do with Iran's uranium, remain largely unresolved.

items.headline: Iran began restoring internet access to tens of millions of people
items.blurb: Iran began restoring internet access to tens of millions of people after a monthslong blackout, officials said.

items.headline: Israel intensified its military strikes against Hezbollah in Lebanon
items.blurb: Israel intensified its military strikes against Hezbollah in Lebanon and advanced deeper into Lebanese territory.

items.headline: U.S. missile found to have killed 21 civilians in Iran
items.blurb: Our Visual Investigations team found evidence that a new type of U.S. missile, which explodes and spreads thousands of deadly pellets, killed 21 civilians in a residential neighborhood in Iran. Watch the video.

items.headline: Trump goes to the doctor
items.blurb: Trump, the oldest person ever to become president, had a physical exam today at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. "Everything checked out PERFECTLY," he wrote on social media, though the White House has not released details to support his claim. The president's health has come under significant scrutiny.

items.headline: Unchain Uncle Sam / America's economy is soaring—even with the MAGA tax
items.blurb: The country's world-beating performance comes with a handicap

items.headline: How much is Donald Trump costing America's economy?
items.blurb: In 2024 we published a cover story declaring America's economy the "envy of the world". And actually, for all the chaos of the past year, it's still showing up its peers. But it's doing so despite, not because of, the MAGA tax—what we call Donald Trump's harmful policies. His successor should unwind them.

items.headline: Why science is becoming less innovative / A huge study suggests ageing scientists are part of the problem
items.blurb: A few years ago a study concluded that science was producing fewer breakthroughs and more incremental advances. New research proposes an explanation: ageing scientists.

items.headline: Inside Defence: Bill Burns on Iran, China, Israel and Hamas
items.blurb: Few people have had more experience of difficult diplomatic negotiations—with Iran, with China, with Israel and Hamas—than Bill Burns. The former ambassador and head of the CIA spoke to Shashank Joshi, our defence editor, for Inside Defence.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Two major threads dominated the day's political news. In Texas, primary results came in through the evening [3], culminating in a significant upset: Attorney General Ken Paxton defeated incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican Senate runoff [2]. Separately, redistricting battles played out in two Southern states. A federal court struck down Alabama's newly drawn congressional map, ruling it unfair to Black voters [5]. In South Carolina, the state Senate defied pressure from former President Trump and declined to advance a new district map [4], leaving the state's political boundaries unchanged for now.

On the public safety front, a chemical tank incident in Southern California prompted evacuation orders for nearby residents, but authorities lifted those orders by late evening after the tank cooled and the immediate danger passed [1].
